column3: It repeats the exact manifest-misguidance formula as a retrospective recognition of a gravely mistaken allegiance.
The wise Quran supplies the authoritative message against which the believer's conclusion in the same surah is framed.
It concerns manifest sin through fabricating against God, but does not address rival objects of worship or misguidance directly.
It preserves the conditional claim that following a lone messenger would be misguidance, a hostile counterclaim to 36:24.
The messenger's authority in the same opening passage supports the message the believer accepts, though indirectly.
The manifest misleading enemy offers a secondary model of misdirection, not the focus's reasoning about worship.
Its rejected reading marks an ironic misguidance accusation, clarifying that the formula alone cannot establish a sound judgment.
The same surah's unresponsive audience explains why the village's warning, and the believer's argument, meet resistance.
It states that an attempt to mislead others rebounds on its authors, illuminating the self-destructive result the believer avoids.
Abraham explicitly identifies taking idols as manifest misguidance, directly paralleling the focus's rejection of gods besides God.
It identifies those who heed the reminder and fear the Merciful, the receptive stance exemplified by the believer.
Refusing God's caller and relying on protectors besides Him is called manifest misguidance, closely matching the focus's argument about futile intercession.
It presents messenger-led teaching as release from prior manifest misguidance, supplying the corrective path.
It begins the village parable whose believing man speaks at 36:24, providing essential narrative setting.
It calls associating creatures with God manifest misguidance, directly supporting the focus's refusal to take others as gods.
It parallels 62:2: a messenger teaches and purifies people formerly in manifest misguidance.
The three envoys establish the mission the believer defends, but add less than the surrounding parable cards.
It shows fabricated objects of reliance vanishing while their adherents lose themselves, sharpening the focus's warning about powerless intercessors.
The prophet says he would be among wrongdoers if he claimed what he does not claim; only the conditional self-implication is parallel.
The villagers reject revelation and accuse the envoys of lying, the denial answered by the believer's later reasoning.
It is another mistaken social accusation of misguidance, but lacks the focus's monotheistic reasoning.
It explicitly says worshipping those invoked besides God and following desires would be misguidance, an especially close conditional parallel.
The envoys reaffirm their commission, advancing the narrative that the believer later endorses.
The elite call Noah manifestly misguided, a contrast showing how established power can misapply the focus's formula to a messenger.
Delayed repentance at death does not clarify manifest misguidance or reliance on other gods.
The envoys' duty of clear delivery explains the public warning to which the believer responds.
The clear Book theme supports intelligible guidance generally, but adds no specific account of the focus's error.
Gratitude, parental care, and repentance do not add a focused relation to the verse.
The villagers' threat against the envoys displays the hostile response surrounding the believer's intervention.
It directly contrasts guidance with manifest misguidance under the shared acknowledgment that God alone provides sustenance.
A clear warning is only a general prophetic-role parallel.
The envoys return the villagers' superstition to their own excess, preparing the diagnosis of their misdirected response.
Its rejected dispute-over-the-Hour reading concerns distant misguidance, not the focus's worship decision.
It records a family dismissing present evidence through an inherited charge of misguidance, a caution about mislabeling.
The immediately preceding verse gives the focus's premise: worship the Creator to whom all return.
Guidance after being lost is a broad opposite movement, without the focus's manifest or worship-related framing.
Abraham calls his people and their fathers manifestly misguided for idol worship, directly corroborating the focus's conclusion.
The light and clear Book offer general guidance but do not specifically explain the focus's error or intercession claim.
The unfair division critique does not add a material relation after stronger idolatry parallels.
The clear Book is a broad source-of-guidance parallel already represented by earlier clear-message cards.
Human loss is too general to explain the particular manifest misguidance in the focus.
It concerns God nullifying the deeds of those who bar His path, only generally related to being misled.
It distinguishes available guidance from an audience unable or unwilling to receive it while in manifest misguidance.
It denies that the messenger is misguided, providing a direct counterpoint to hostile misguidance accusations.
Revelation and clear warning explain prophetic communication generally, but add little to the focus's monotheistic inference.
It records rejecters accusing warners of great misguidance and later acknowledging their own failure, a strong reversal parallel.
It calls present wrongdoers manifestly misguided despite their later hearing and seeing, emphasizing culpable refusal of guidance.
It contrasts divine steadiness for believers with the misguiding of wrongdoers, but does not identify the focus's specific cause.
The righteous being in bliss has no focused contribution to the argument about misguidance.
The clear Quran is a redundant general source-of-guidance link.
Faith and reliance on the Merciful are set against manifest misguidance, closely echoing the focus's trust in God rather than others.
Pharaoh misleads his people instead of guiding them, furnishing a concrete opposite to true divine direction.
It explicitly distinguishes the bearer of guidance from one in manifest misguidance, though without the focus's worship rationale.
It broadly contrasts God's guidance with being left without a guide, adding less after closer parallels.
The same opponents call believers manifestly misguided while refusing God's command, directly extending the village's reversal of accusation.
Slipping after clear signs is a general image of departing a shown path, not a close inter-ayah explanation.
Another social verdict of manifest misguidance illustrates the formula's use as accusation rather than a direct theological parallel.
Following desire without knowledge and lacking protectors explains a route to misguidance opposed to the focus's reasoned worship.
Hardened hearts unable to receive the reminder are called manifestly misguided, explaining the kind of refusal surrounding the parable.
Clear verses and divine guidance are a general corrective, already supplied more specifically by earlier cards.
The challenge concerning the soul at death does not clarify the focus's stated misguidance.
Its manifest falsehood concerns rumor and communal trust rather than worship or divine guidance.
A clear warner is a generic role parallel with little marginal value after the local envoys.
It links misguidance to inherited following, a plausible background to the villagers' resistance but not an explicit focus parallel.
A clear messenger and rejected reminder repeat the warning-response pattern already well covered.
It contrasts those who stray from God's path with those rightly guided, while grounding the distinction in God's knowledge.
Divine clarification is a broad linguistic counterpart to 'manifest,' but does not address misguidance.
Moses describes a past act as being among the misguided, showing the formula can mark a limited prior condition rather than a fixed identity.
Fleeing to God rejects the direction away from Him, but is only an indirect monotheistic parallel.
A manifest sign supports prophetic proof generally, not the focus's diagnosis of worship as error.
It describes a futile call after rejecting messengers with clear proofs, echoing the focus's claim that other intercession cannot save.
Rejecters refuse to abandon their gods while demanding proof, directly displaying the rival-worship stance the focus rejects.
Mockery of resurrection does not add a focused relation to the verse.
The damned identify criminals as those who led them astray, adding a downstream account of misguiding influence.
A manifest authority against arrogance is a remote proof-and-warning parallel.
Choosing misguidance over guidance gives a general decision model but is redundant after closer conditional choices.
A clear warner is another generic messenger-role statement.
It distinguishes one's own guidance from another's misguidance, but does not illuminate worship or intercession.
Disobeying God and His messenger is explicitly called manifest misguidance, directly connecting error to rejecting a settled divine command.
The clear-warner role is already established by more proximate narrative and formula parallels.
It explicitly forbids setting another god beside God, the central alternative rejected by the believer in 36:24.
Verifying reports before action is unrelated to the focus's worship and rescue reasoning.
It joins being misguided with denying truth, a relevant but broad description of the focus's opposing stance.
Marriage limits and their explanation do not contribute to the focus's argument.
The teaching of expression is too abstract to add to manifest misguidance after stronger clarity cards.
The explanation of legal signs is not a focused parallel to the verse.
Calling clear proofs magic illustrates rejecting evidence, but the setting is remote and redundant.
It denies sufficiency to rival objects and says the misled have no guide, partially echoing the focus's rejection of other protectors.
Persistent doubt after clear proofs is tied to God's misguiding of the excessive doubter, explaining continued refusal of guidance.
Changing God's blessing after clear signs is a broad rejection pattern, without a direct link to the focus's reasoning.
The breathing dawn has no focused relation to the verse.
The explanation of gambling, wine, and spending does not illuminate manifest misguidance here.
A manifest horizon is a different use of clarity and adds no substantive relation.
Making rivals for God in order to mislead from His way directly parallels the focus's rejection of other gods.
The promise not to let martyrs' deeds go astray is unrelated to the focus's claim.
Taking devils as protectors besides God while thinking oneself guided closely explains the misplaced reliance condemned in the focus.
Testimony at a deathbed does not add a focused relation to manifest misguidance.
It defends a clear warner against a madness charge, a distant instance of resisting false labels.
Human reactions to mercy and adversity do not clarify the focus's conclusion.
Pharaoh's wealth and splendor become means of leading people from God's path, a concrete mechanism of misguidance.
The believer enters the parable by urging his people to follow the messengers, immediately setting up the reasoning voiced in 36:24.
It identifies the messengers as seeking no reward and as rightly guided, the direct grounds for the believer's subsequent alignment.
The immediately preceding question rejects gods besides God because their intercession cannot avert harm or save, directly completing the conditional conclusion of 36:24.
The believer's declaration of faith in the Lord states the committed alternative to the manifest misguidance he has just rejected.
Later in the same surah, taking gods besides God in hope of help supplies the collective counterpart to the believer's rejected alternative.
It denies that those gods can help their worshippers, directly echoing the focus's claim that their intercession and rescue are powerless.
It asks whether to invoke besides God what neither benefits nor harms, and links doing so with being turned back after guidance.
It names worship of what neither harms nor benefits besides God and the claim that such beings are intercessors.
It forbids invoking besides God what neither benefits nor harms, with wrongdoing as the consequence of doing so.
It rejects worship of names besides God and directs judgment and worship to God alone.
Those invoked besides God cannot remove or alter harm, closely paralleling the focus's test of supposed intercession.
Abraham challenges worship of what cannot benefit or harm, directly expressing the focus's criterion for rejecting other gods.
Calling upon what neither harms nor benefits besides God is explicitly called far misguidance.
Calling another god alongside God is condemned as an unsupported claim, reinforcing the focus's exclusive worship.
The alleged gods besides God cannot create, control death, life, or resurrection, directly exposing their incapacity.
Those called besides God possess nothing and share no power with Him, directly undermining reliance on them.
Intercession avails only by God's permission, providing the general limit presupposed in the focus's denial of saving intercession.
Those invoked besides God possess no share of dominion, explaining why they cannot provide the rescue imagined in 36:23.
Those invoked besides God neither hear nor answer their callers and will disavow the association, directly negating reliance on them.
Taking protectors besides God to gain nearness presents the same misplaced mediating reliance that the focus rejects.
It tests the alleged powers besides God against His intending harm, closely matching the focus's conditional test of rescue.
It rebukes taking intercessors besides God even when they possess no power or understanding, an exact thematic parallel.
It assigns all intercession to God alone, clarifying why rival intercessors cannot save in the focus.
Those invoked besides God possess no power of intercession except under the stated condition, directly qualifying the focus's claim.
It calls no one more astray than one who invokes besides God beings unable to answer, a direct diagnosis of the focus's rejected act.
The gods taken as means of nearness fail their worshippers and disappear, a narrative outcome of the focus's argument.
Even angelic intercession does not avail except after God's permission, reinforcing the inability of unapproved intermediaries to save.
It commands that none be invoked alongside God, directly affirming the exclusive worship assumed by the believer.
The messenger disclaims power over harm or right direction, reinforcing that rescue and guidance cannot be assigned to other beings.
